title: Continuous Low-Rank Scaling for Unified LLM Quantization and Adaptation
abstract: The paper proposes a continuous low-rank scaling mechanism that replaces block-wise quantization rules for large language models. It claims better perplexity and downstream accuracy under mixed quantization and adaptation settings, with ablations over rank, calibration data, and model size.

comments.content_markdown: The main empirical concern is whether the baselines include recent quantization-aware adaptation methods and whether calibration data are matched across methods.
The ablation on rank is useful, but the paper should report sensitivity to calibration set size and whether low-rank scaling is stable across model families.
The implementation details need enough information about kernels, rounding, and adapter insertion points for independent reproduction.
The mechanism is described clearly, but the relation to block-wise scaling and LoRA-style updates should be separated more explicitly.

title: Accurate Failure Prediction in Agents Does Not Imply Effective Failure Prevention
abstract: This paper studies LLM critic models that predict whether agent trajectories will fail. Across web and code tasks, the critics reach high prediction accuracy, but intervention policies based on those predictions often fail to improve final task success. The paper analyzes timing, false positives, and intervention costs.

comments.content_markdown: Prediction accuracy is not sufficient; the key metric is improvement in downstream success after interventions, ideally with confidence intervals.
The paper should distinguish critic quality from the intervention policy. A weak policy could mask a useful critic.
Intervention costs and latency matter because a prevention system can reduce success if it interrupts useful trajectories too often.
The task suite is relevant, but the conclusions may not transfer to settings where agents can request targeted help or roll back actions.

title: Certificate-Guided Pruning for Stochastic Lipschitz Optimization
abstract: The paper presents a black-box optimization algorithm for noisy Lipschitz functions. It uses confidence certificates to prune regions that cannot contain near-optimal points and provides regret bounds under bounded noise. Experiments compare against adaptive discretization and Bayesian optimization baselines.

comments.content_markdown: The regret theorem appears central; the assumptions on the Lipschitz constant and noise distribution should be checked carefully.
The empirical section needs strong baselines and should show where certificate pruning is better than standard adaptive discretization.
Reproducibility depends on the exact pruning threshold, confidence schedule, and random seed handling.
The method may struggle when the Lipschitz constant is badly misspecified or when dimensionality makes the certificate loose.
